3. The plaintiff's further case is that the defendant in the agreement dated 25-9-1991 promised that he would not change the nature and character of the suit premises without permission of the landlord. But in violation of the terms of the agreement the defendant changed the nature thereof. The plaintiff's further alleged that they for construction of a multistoried building got the plan approved by the Comilla Pourashava. The sons of the plaintiffs are leading idle and unemployed life for having no shop of their own for business. As a result it is necessary for the plaintiff's to get vacant possession of the suit premises for his own cause. The plaintiff repeatedly asked the defendant to surrender possession in their favour. But the defendant did not do so. Thereafter the plaintiffs on 3-12-2003 sent notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act determining the landlord tenant relationship and asked him for vacant possession. The plaintiffs having failed to get possession filed the instant suit. 

 5. The further case of the defendant is that the plaintiff by using the Pourashava plan as weapon enhanced the rent for several times and thereafter obtained a new agreement from him. In such a situation the plaintiffs served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act upon the defendant to vacate the premises on the plea of bonafide requirement which he received on 9-1-1991. The plaintiffs some days after through Matbars proposed that if the defendant agree to deposit a handsome amount of security money and further agreed to enhance rent to the tune of Taka 1000 per month he would not be evicted. The defendant was compelled to agree with the proposal of plaintiffs and deposited Taka 75,000 as security money and agreed to pay enhance rent of Taka 1000 per month. Thereafter the plaintiff and the defendant entered into a new agreement signed on 25-1-1991. The defendant came to know subsequently that some illegal and void terms were inserted in the agreement beyond his knowledge. 

 6. The further case of the defendant is that during the continuance of his business in the suit premises the Tin, Partition, Roof Pillar, etc. of the shop room became weak and shaken and rain water used to leak through the tin hole from the roof. The defendant brought this matter to the notice of the plaintiff with a request to repair it. But they permitted the defendant to repair the defects by his own expense which would be adjusted against the rent. The defendant after getting the permission and consent from the plaintiffs started repairing of the suit shop on 28-10-2003 and completed within two months under the active supervision of the plaintiff by spending Taka 2,50,000 and then made decoration of the shop. As a result the suit shop became very much stronger than previous position and also became very beautiful to look at. 

 7. The further case of the defendant is that the plaintiff subsequently became very envious at the beautiful sight of the suit shop and started conspiracy to make the defendant a defaulter and with that end in view stopped receiving rent from the month of November, 2003 despite repeated offer by the defendant and refused to adjust the money which was spent for repairing the suit shop. Then the defendant sent the rent by post which was also refused to accept by the plaintiffs. As a result the defendant had to file a Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 2004 to deposit the monthly rent under Rent Control Ordinance and the same was allowed on 17-6-2004 and thus the defendant is still depositing the rent before the office of rent controller. 

 10. During the course of trial plaintiff examined as many as two witnesses and defendant examined as many as four witnesses to prove their respective cases. Plaintiff himself was examined as PW 1 who approved and exhibited the Comilla Pourashava Plan as Exhibit 1 dated 24-6-66. Next he proved the bharatia agreement dated 25-9-1991 which was exhibited as Exhibit 2 and a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was proved and exhibited as Exhibit 3. The defendant was examined as DW 1 who proved and exhibited the rent receipts as Exhibit Ka. Next he proved and exhibited a series of cash memo for purchasing different goods for repairing the suit shop and examined 3 other witnesses in support of the case of the defendant. 

 13. The learned Counsel Mr Md Asaduzzaman, appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioner, submits that the defendant examined four witnesses to prove their case and all the witnesses categorically corroborated the case of the defendant that as a matter of fact the plaintiff has got no bonafide requirement to get the vacant possession of the suit shop. Next he submits that Pourashave Plan dated 24-6-66 which was submitted by the plaintiff remained valid for six months and after the expiry of six months the plan has become infructuous. The learned Counsel for the defendant-petitioner further submits that the defendant while repairing the suit shop with the consent of the plaintiff he did not ask the defendant to quit the suit shop and after repairing the shop while the defendant decorated the shop by painting and by different fixtures and furniture’s then the plaintiff became greedy and envious to evict the defendant from the said suit shop with a plea to his bonafide requirement that his son will ran a business in the said suit shop. The learned Counsel for the defendant-petitioner finally submits that, as a matter of fact, that the plaintiff has got no cause of action for filing the suit and there was no bonafide requirement of the plaintiff to get the vacant possession of the suit shop. The learned Senior Assistant Judge cum SCC Judge, Sadar, Comilla is absolutely wrong and erroneous in considering that the plaintiff has been able to prove the case to the effect that the plaintiff has got the bonafide requirement of the suit shop and thereby decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff which is liable to be interfered by this Court. 

 14. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr Md Osman Ghani with Mr Muhammad Moshiul Alam, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, submits that the learned Court below is absolutely right and justified in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party and there was no misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record by the learned Senior Assistant Judge-cum-SCC. Judge, Sadar, Comilla. Next he submits that since 24-6-66 on several occasions the plaintiff attempted to construct a multistoried building in the suit premises by demolishing the suit shop along with other shops but all the time it is due to the resistance of the defendant-petitioner he could not execute the plan. To prove the bonafides of intention of the plaintiff some RCC Pillar has already been constructed in pursuance of the Pourashava Plan approved on 24-6-66 which is very much apparent on the site. The learned Counsel next submits that DW 1, in his cross-examination, admitted that three plaintiffs have got total thirteen sons and among the thirteen sons three sons have been provided, two sons are serving abroad and one is doing business in the country and rest of them are unemployed and for this reason the plaintiffs decided to construct a multistoried building and to provide each of them with a shop to run business and with this end in view the plaintiff since long attempted on several occasions to execute his plan but due to the resistance of the defendant, the plaintiff could not execute his plan. The learned Counsel finally submits that the plaintiff has been able to successfully prove his case by producing documentary evidence as well as by adducing oral evidence and the learned Court below committed no error or illegality in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff, hence the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge-cum-SCC Judge, Sadar, Comilla is not liable to be interfered by this Court in revision, as such, the Rule should be discharged. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-opposite party referred the case of Jahanara Khatun vs Md Nurul Islam reported in 12 MLR (AD) 241 = 59 DLR 64 wherein has been held: 

 15. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, exhibits and documents produced by both the parties and the judgment of the trial Court and the bharatia agreement it appears that the plaintiff landlord served notice upon the defendant-tenant by invoking Clause No. 4 of the Agreement to hand over vacant possession of the suit shop and terminated the deed of bharatia agreement. The plaintiff has been able to prove his case by documentary evidence and also by adducing oral evidence. PW 2 Latu Mia was a signatory of the agreement deed was also a tenant and shop-keeper of the landlord who stated in his evidence that the plaintiff submitted a plan for approval by the Comilla Municipality and the plan duly approved by the Municipality and some RCC Pillars have already been constructed. This witness fully corroborates the evidence of PW 1. It appears that there is no misreading, non-reading and non-consideration of the material evidence on record by the trial Court. 

 16. By now the settled principle of law in exercising the revisional power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also under section 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act have been laid down in several judicial pronouncements of our Appellate Division that the finding of facts whether concurrent or not arrived at by the lower appellate Court is final unless it is manifestly perverse. In this connection I like to rely on the decision in the case of Hazari Bala Sana vs Niron alias Niranjan Mondal reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 294 wherein it has been held: 

 "It is a settled principle that the finding of fact, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court, which is the final Court of fact, is binding on the High Court Division, as a revisional Court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case." 

 17. The judgment of the learned trial Court transpires that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully examined all the material facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, including the bharatia agreement deed affecting the merit of the case. The learned Counsel of the defendant-petitioner also could not point out any error or illegality or infirmity of law in the judgment passed by the learned trial Court. 

 18. In view of the discussion made above and the facts and circumstances of the case and also the legal position the impugned judgment and decree dated 23-1-2006 and 30-1-2006 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge-cum SCC Judge, Sadar, Comilla decreeing the SCC. Suit No. 1 of 2004 with cost and the case having been concluded on finding of facts, as such, no interference is called for in revision under section 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act.
